title: Wind Resource and Weibull Distribution
text:
Current Method
The background model describes fitting approximately ten years of offshore wind observations from the Dutch Offshore Wind Atlas (Dutch Offshore Wind Atlas, n.d.) to a Weibull distribution and wind rose.
For each wind state, the model evaluates turbine output and wake losses. The annual yield is then obtained by weighting the power output of each state by its probability.

title: Wind Resource and Weibull Distribution
text:
Energy Balance
The wind resource page does not apply conversion losses directly. It supplies gross turbine power states to downstream components:

electricity components apply electrical efficiency and availability factors
hydrogen production evaluates stack efficiency and balance-of-plant losses at each operating point
compression power depends on hydrogen flow and pressure ratio

title: Wind Resource and Layout
text:
This section documents the wind resource, wake modelling, spacing, and infield-layout assumptions that determine gross energy production and infrastructure length.
The wind-resource and layout model connects the physical site to component sizing. Turbine positions determine wake losses and infield network geometry. Wake-aware production determines both annual yield and the operating points of hydrogen conversion equipment.

title: Wind Turbine
text:
Energy Balance
The turbine power curve and wake model determine gross turbine output. For the electricity configuration, the turbine output measurement is treated as being after the inverter and before the internal transformer. The transformer is included in total turbine cost but its efficiency is accounted for in the electrical chain.
For decentralised hydrogen, the electrical conversion chain differs because the PEM stack can connect to the turbine DC link rather than using the full inverter-transformer path.

title: Turbine System
text:
The turbine system includes the wind turbine, generator, turbine-side power electronics, tower and nacelle mass, and foundation.
The turbine system is common to all architectures at the level of aerodynamic energy capture, but the downstream electrical conversion chain changes between electricity, centralised hydrogen, and decentralised hydrogen.

title: Turbine System
text:
Current Baseline
The current model uses a 15 MW turbine as the baseline unit. Turbine and foundation assumptions are documented separately because foundations, tower mass, and installation costs can scale with mass and structural loading.

title: Foundation
text:
Energy Balance
The foundation has no direct energy conversion role. Its effect enters through CAPEX, installation cost, OPEX, and potentially availability if future assumptions add foundation-related downtime.

title: Foundation
text:
Availability
No separate foundation availability factor is currently applied. Foundation-related downtime is implicitly included in the turbine or farm-level availability assumptions unless modelled otherwise.

title: Foundation
text:
Mass and Scaling
The current foundation cost is fixed per 15 MW turbine. A future refinement should connect foundation cost to turbine rating, water depth, soil condition, tower/nacelle mass, and hydrogen equipment mass where relevant.

title: Scaling Laws
text:
Discrete Scaling
Some infrastructure is discrete rather than continuously scalable:

HVDC export capacity follows 2 GW block logic in the current source framing.
Export pipelines are selected from discrete diameter and pressure options.
Stack modules are 2.5 MW units.

Discrete scaling can create optima where slightly lower yield is accepted to avoid adding another large component.

title: Financial Assumptions
text:
LCOE Treatment
Annualised CAPEX, annual OPEX, and annual delivered energy are combined as:
LCOE = (annualised_CAPEX + annual_OPEX) / annual_delivered_energy
Hydrogen may also be reported in EUR/kg, but the common comparison basis is EUR/MWh using HHV.

title: Financial Assumptions
text:
Inflation and Currency
Some hydrogen component costs are derived from NREL values (Badgett et al. 2024) in 2020 USD, converted to 2025 EUR, and increased with a 50% markup to represent sales price instead of production cost.
This conversion convention should be made explicit for every imported cost source.

title: Platform and Substation Installation
text:
This page calculates the offshore installation CAPEX of a conventionally crane-installed, piled-jacket offshore substation (OSS). The result is needed to convert the separately costed jacket, piles and topside into an installed offshore asset without hiding transport, vessel occupation or commissioning inside the fabrication cost.
The calculation separates four work packages:

foundation piles and, for pre-piling, the positioning template;
jacket transport, lift, set-down and structural connection;
topside transport, lift, set-down and structural connection; and
offshore hook-up, testing and commissioning.

These packages may share a mobilisation or vessel in a project execution plan, but they do not share a universal rate or productivity. The model is not applicable without a method change to float-over topsides, gravity bases, self-installing platforms or ultra-heavy single-lift systems.






ImportantFeasibility precedes cost



A lift or transport arrangement that fails a capacity, geometry or stability check is not represented by adding installation days. The model must select another vessel class or installation method before calculating duration and cost.

text:
Lift and Transport Feasibility
For lift unit \(j\), the crane-capacity gate is
\[
\gamma_{\mathrm{dyn},j}\left(m_j+m_{\mathrm{rig},j}\right)
\leq
SWL(R_j,\mathrm{config}_j),
\]
with the geometry gates
\[
H_{\mathrm{hook}}
\geq H_{\mathrm{required},j},
\qquad
R_{\mathrm{available}}
\geq R_j.
\]
For the selected installation vessel or deck carrier,
\[
m_j+m_{\mathrm{seafast},j}\leq M_{\mathrm{use}},
\qquad
\frac{B_jL_j}{f_{\mathrm{pack}}}\leq A_{\mathrm{use}},
\qquad
p_{\mathrm{local},j}\leq p_{\mathrm{deck,max}}.
\]
Here \(m_j\), \(m_{\mathrm{rig},j}\) and \(m_{\mathrm{seafast},j}\) are the lift-unit, rigging and seafastening masses in tonnes; \(\gamma_{\mathrm{dyn},j}\) is the dimensionless engineered dynamic factor; \(SWL\) is the crane safe working load in tonnes at radius \(R_j\) and the stated configuration; \(H_{\mathrm{hook}}\) and \(H_{\mathrm{required},j}\) are available and required hook heights in metres; \(B_j\) and \(L_j\) are cargo dimensions in metres; \(f_{\mathrm{pack}}\) is the usable packing fraction; \(M_{\mathrm{use}}\) and \(A_{\mathrm{use}}\) are usable carrier mass and area; and \(p_{\mathrm{local},j}\) and \(p_{\mathrm{deck,max}}\) are actual and allowable local deck loads.
The engineered check must also cover centre of gravity, lifting-point loads, tandem synchronisation, boom and structure clearance, under-hook rigging, carrier stability, quay load-out, water depth, vessel draft, air gap and DP or mooring footprint.
Public fleet specifications illustrate discontinuous capability classes rather than default vessel choices: Rambiz and Gulliver are reported at 3,300 t and 4,000 t tandem capacity (Scaldis Salvage and Marine Contractors, n.d.); Saipem 7000 at 14,000 t combined capacity (Saipem, n.d.); and Sleipnir at 20,000 t tandem capacity with a 220 m by 102 m reinforced deck (Heerema Marine Contractors, n.d.). Pioneering Spirit reports separate 60,000 t topside and 20,000 t jacket systems (Allseas, n.d.). Actual radius, lift path and configuration always govern.

title: Cable and Pipeline Installation
text:
1. How an Installation Campaign Works
Offshore installation converts supplied cable or pipe into a connected, protected and tested offshore asset. A typical cable campaign proceeds as follows:
mobilise the installation spread → load product at port → transit to site → survey or prepare the route → pull in the first end → lay the product → return to port and splice when required → pull in the second end → bury the route → inspect and survey the installation → test and complete the asset → demobilise
The activities are not always strictly sequential. Pull-ins occur around individual lay sections, not only after the complete route has been laid. An export-cable splice can interrupt laying when another product length is loaded. Burial and post-burial survey normally follow as separate campaigns in the reference method.
This page uses one time-and-rate framework for four installation subclasses:

66–132 kV inter-array cables;
320–525 kV HVDC export systems;
spoolable thermoplastic-composite-pipe (TCP) hydrogen infield pipelines; and
spoolable TCP hydrogen export pipelines.

The accounting framework is shared. Product configuration, task times, installation rates and feasibility limits remain subclass-specific.
Cost boundary
The installation boundary begins when the contracted spreads mobilise and ends after the offshore testing included in their installation scope.







Scope
Treatment




Cable or pipe manufacture and supply accessories
Excluded; owned by the relevant cable or pipeline page


Lay-spread mobilisation, loading, transit, laying, pull-ins, offshore splices, lay-spread testing and demobilisation
Included through lay-spread time


Burial-spread mobilisation, transit, trenching or burial, positioning and demobilisation
Included through burial-spread time


Independent ROV and survey campaigns or support
Included through ROV/survey-spread time


Crew, fuel, routine workboats and tugs, and contractor overhead

text:
3. Physical Quantities and Installation Configuration
ORBIT can estimate installation time only after the physical system and installation method have been configured correctly. Three length measures remain distinct.








Quantity
Definition
Model use




Route-kilometre
Horizontal centreline distance between route endpoints
Defines the corridor


Physical cable- or pipeline-kilometre
Total product installed across every distinct asset
Controls product mass, loading and supplied length


Pass-kilometre
Distance travelled while one physical cable or pipeline is installed
Controls lay and burial time; survey passes are counted separately



For asset type \(a\), physical length is:
\[
L_{\mathrm{physical},a}
=
N_{\mathrm{parallel},a}L_{\mathrm{route},a}(1+s_a)
+L_{\mathrm{vert},a}.
\]








Symbol
Definition
Unit




\(N_{\mathrm{parallel},a}\)
Number of distinct physical cables or pipes
count


\(L_{\mathrm{route},a}\)
Horizontal route length
route-km


\(s_a\)

dimensionless


\(L_{\mathrm{vert},a}\)
Total separately calculated vertical and structure allowance
km


\(L_{\mathrm{physical},a}\)

physical km



Slack is not added when project section lengths already include it.
ORBIT installs every array-cable section and export cable individually. The reference model therefore permits only one physical cable or pipeline in each lay or burial pass. For spread type \(x\):
\[
N_{\mathrm{pass},x,a}
=
N_{\mathrm{parallel},a},
\qquad
L_{\mathrm{pass},x,a}
=
N_{\mathrm{pass},x,a}L_{\mathrm{route},a}.
\]
For non-identical sections or routes, actual traversed lengths are summed:
\[
L_{\mathrm{pass},x}
=
\sum_m L_m.
\]
Here \(x\) identifies the lay or burial spread, \(N_{\mathrm{pass},x,a}\) is its pass count and \(L_{\mathrm{pass},x,a}\) is pass-km. Survey length is calculated from its own required route passes because a survey can cover a corridor rather than every individual product.
TenneT calls its 2 GW export connection one cable system, but defines that system as four individual cables: positive pole, negative pole, metallic return and fibre-optic cable (TenneT, n.d.). Under the one-cable-per-pass ORBIT convention, one TenneT reference system therefore contains four physical lay units and four lay passes. Product length, mass and loading are calculated separately for each cable type; the indicative power-cable mass is not applied to the metallic return or fibre cable. This is a transparent screening convention, not evidence that TenneT’s contractor necessarily installs the four-cable bundle in four separate operations.

title: Cable and Pipeline Installation
text:
4. Lay-Spread Time
The lay-spread calculation follows ORBIT’s cable-installation task logic. ORBIT explicitly represents mobilisation, product loading, vessel storage, port returns, route laying, positioning, pull-ins, offshore splicing, termination/testing and transit (National Laboratory of the Rockies, n.d.). Demobilisation remains a separate unresolved input because the reviewed cable module does not contain a general demobilisation task.
Chargeable lay time is divided into port or other non-weather-uplifted time and offshore weather-exposed time:
\[
T_{\mathrm{lay,base}}
=
T_{\mathrm{lay,nonweather}}
+T_{\mathrm{lay,offshore,base}}.
\]








Symbol
Definition
Unit




\(T_{\mathrm{lay,base}}\)
Lay time before weather uplift
day


\(T_{\mathrm{lay,nonweather}}\)
Port and other defined lay time not exposed to the offshore weather uplift
day


\(T_{\mathrm{lay,offshore,base}}\)
Offshore-exposed lay time before weather uplift
day



Weather is applied later, after all base tasks have been counted.
Product per load
The mass-limited product length is usable vessel capacity divided by product linear mass:
\[
L_{\mathrm{load,mass}}
=
\frac{M_{\mathrm{usable}}}{\lambda_{\mathrm{product}}}.
\]
Actual product per load is the lowest applicable limit:
\[
L_{\mathrm{load}}
=
\min\left(
L_{\mathrm{load,mass}},
L_{\mathrm{reel/partition}},
L_{\mathrm{manufacturing}},
L_{\mathrm{handling}}
\right).
\]








Symbol
Definition
Unit




\(M_{\mathrm{usable}}\)
Usable product mass on the lay vessel
t


\(\lambda_{\mathrm{product}}\)
Product linear mass
t/physical km


\(L_{\mathrm{reel/partition}}\)
Reel, carousel or partition limit
physical km/load


\(L_{\mathrm{manufacturing}}\)
Available continuous manufactured length
physical km/load


\(L_{\mathrm{handling}}\)
Handling or installation-analysis limit
physical km/load


\(L_{\mathrm{load}}\)
Effective product length per load
physical km/load


\(L_{\mathrm{physical},m}\)
Physical product length of lay unit \(m\)
physical km


\(N_{\mathrm{load},m}\)
Loads for lay unit \(m\), including its initial load
count


\(N_{\mathrm{reload},m}\)
Loads after the initial load for lay unit \(m\)
count


\(N_{\mathrm{load}}\), \(N_{\mathrm{reload}}\)
Campaign totals summed over physical lay units
count



If products with different linear masses share a load, loaded mass is calculated product by product rather than by applying one average linear mass.
The ORBIT reference carousel has a 13,000 t maximum mass. The screening calculation uses \(M_{\mathrm{usable}}=13{,}000\) t, while retaining the reel, manufacturing and handling limits in the minimum above. For example, an indicative 65 t/km HVDC pole cable would be mass-limited to 200 physical km/load. That result is not transferred to the metallic-return or fibre-optic cables.
Loads are calculated separately for every physical lay unit \(m\), so that each cable or pipeline receives one initial load and uses its own mass and handling limits:
\[
N_{\mathrm{load},m}
=
\left\lceil
\frac{L_{\mathrm{physical},m}}{L_{\mathrm{load},m}}
\right\rceil,
\qquad
N_{\mathrm{reload},m}
=
\max(0,N_{\mathrm{load},m}-1).
\]
Campaign totals are:
\[
N_{\mathrm{load}}=\sum_m N_{\mathrm{load},m},
\qquad
N_{\mathrm{reload}}=\sum_m N_{\mathrm{reload},m}.
\]
Port loading time is therefore:
\[
T_{\mathrm{port\ load}}
=
\sum_m
\left(
t_{\mathrm{initial\ load},m}
+N_{\mathrm{reload},m}t_{\mathrm{reload\ load},m}
\right).
\]
Here \(t_{\mathrm{initial\ load},m}\) and \(t_{\mathrm{reload\ load},m}\) are chargeable port-loading times in days. Under the ORBIT screening values both equal 6/24 day. A TenneT system with four physical cable passes therefore has four initial loads even when every cable fits on one vessel load.
ORBIT uses six hours for both the initial load and each reload (National Laboratory of the Rockies, n.d.). This is product-loading time only. It does not include the return transit and repositioning needed for a reload.
Port returns
For one-way distance \(D_{\mathrm{port}}\) between the work site and loading port, vessel transit speed \(v_{\mathrm{transit}}\) in km/h and repositioning time \(t_{\mathrm{reposition}}\) in days:
\[
T_{\mathrm{port\ return}}
=
\sum_m N_{\mathrm{reload},m}
\left(
\frac{2D_{\mathrm{port}}}{24v_{\mathrm{transit}}}
+t_{\mathrm{reposition}}
\right).
\]
The port loading itself remains in \(T_{\mathrm{port\ load}}\), so it is not included again in this expression.
The ORBIT reference cable vessel uses \(v_{\mathrm{transit}}=11.5\) km/h. Its reload sequence includes the outbound and return transits; onsite positioning associated with an offshore splice is counted in the splice task below and is not added as \(t_{\mathrm{reposition}}\).
Route laying
Lay production time is lay pass-km divided by the selected operating lay rate:
\[
T_{\mathrm{route\ lay}}
=
\sum_j
\frac{L_{\mathrm{pass,lay},j}}{q_{\mathrm{lay},j}}.
\]
The reviewed ORBIT version 1.3 implementation uses \(q_{\mathrm{lay}}=0.4\) km/h, equivalent to 9.6 km/day of continuous operation (National Laboratory of the Rockies, n.d.). This is an operating rate, not an achieved weather-inclusive campaign rate. Product handling, stops, interfaces and weather are represented separately.
Pull-ins, splicing and testing
ORBIT divides cable interfaces into positioning, preparation, pull-in, termination/testing, lowering and, when required, cable recovery and splicing. The time for any repeated interface task \(u\) is:
\[
T_u
=
\frac{N_u t_u}{24}.
\]
The sourced task values are:








Task \(u\)
\(t_u\)
Counting rule




Position onsite
2 h/location
Once at the start of each array section and at the offshore end of an export cable; also included in each splice sequence


Prepare cable
1 h/event
At each array-cable end and at export landfall


Pull in cable
5.5 h/end
At every modeled pull-in or pull-up


Terminate and test
5.5 h/end
At every end while the lay spread remains occupied


Lower cable
1 h/event
After the first-end sequence and after a splice


Raise cable
0.5 h/splice
Before an offshore splice


Splice cable
48 h/splice
Between continuous export-cable loads



Using those task counts, the complete interface term is:
\[
T_{\mathrm{interface}}
=
\frac{
2N_{\mathrm{position}}
+N_{\mathrm{prepare}}
+5.5N_{\mathrm{pull}}
+5.5N_{\mathrm{termination}}
+N_{\mathrm{lower}}
}{24}.
\]
Each offshore splice additionally occupies the lay spread for positioning, cable recovery, splicing and lowering:
\[
T_{\mathrm{splice}}
=
N_{\mathrm{splice}}
\frac{2+0.5+48+1}{24}
=
N_{\mathrm{splice}}\frac{51.5}{24}.
\]
These values are executable ORBIT defaults (National Laboratory of the Rockies, n.d.). They apply only when the lay spread remains occupied. An array-cable section uses two pull-ins and two termination/test tasks; an export cable uses a landfall sequence and an offshore-end sequence. The exact event counts remain derived from the physical installation inventory rather than embedded in a kilometre rate.
For array cables, a reload normally supplies additional discrete cable sections and does not automatically create an offshore splice. For a continuous export route, exceeding the available continuous product length can require both a reload and an inline splice.
Lay-time aggregation
Non-weather-uplifted lay time is:
\[
T_{\mathrm{lay,nonweather}}
=
T_{\mathrm{mob,lay}}
+T_{\mathrm{port\ load}}
+T_{\mathrm{demob,lay}}.
\]
Base offshore-exposed lay time is:
\[
\begin{aligned}
T_{\mathrm{lay,offshore,base}}
={}&
T_{\mathrm{site\ transit}}
+T_{\mathrm{route\ lay}}
+T_{\mathrm{port\ return}}\\
&+T_{\mathrm{position}}
+T_{\mathrm{interface}}
+T_{\mathrm{splice}}
\end{aligned}
\]
All terms in the two aggregation equations are chargeable days. \(T_{\mathrm{mob,lay}}\) is 1.5 full-rate-equivalent days in the cable screening case, representing ORBIT’s three calendar days at 50% of the day rate. \(T_{\mathrm{demob,lay}}\) remains unresolved. \(T_{\mathrm{site\ transit}}\) is initial offshore transit, and \(T_{\mathrm{position}}\) contains only positioning not already included in \(T_{\mathrm{interface}}\) or \(T_{\mathrm{splice}}\). Every task is assigned once.

title: Cable and Pipeline Installation
text:
5. Burial-Spread Time
The reference method uses a separate burial spread. Its task sequence is mobilisation, transit, tool deployment and setup, burial or pre-trenching passes, repositioning, tool recovery and demobilisation.
Non-weather-uplifted burial time is mobilisation and demobilisation:
\[
T_{\mathrm{bury,nonweather}}
=
T_{\mathrm{mob,bury}}
+T_{\mathrm{demob,bury}}.
\]
Base offshore-exposed burial time is:
\[
\begin{aligned}
T_{\mathrm{bury,offshore,base}}
={}&
T_{\mathrm{transit,bury}}
+T_{\mathrm{setup,bury}}\\
&+\sum_j
\frac{L_{\mathrm{pass,bury},j}}{q_{\mathrm{bury},j}}
+T_{\mathrm{reposition,bury}}\\
&+T_{\mathrm{recovery,bury}}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore:
\[
T_{\mathrm{bury,base}}
=
T_{\mathrm{bury,nonweather}}
+T_{\mathrm{bury,offshore,base}}.
\]

Definition
Unit




\(T_{\mathrm{bury,base}}\)
Total burial time before weather uplift
day


\(T_{\mathrm{bury,nonweather}}\)
Fixed burial-spread time outside the offshore weather uplift
day


\(T_{\mathrm{bury,offshore,base}}\)
Offshore-exposed burial time before weather uplift
day


\(T_{\mathrm{mob,bury}}\), \(T_{\mathrm{demob,bury}}\)
Burial-spread mobilisation and demobilisation
day


\(T_{\mathrm{transit,bury}}\)
Burial-spread offshore transit
day


\(L_{\mathrm{pass,bury},j}\)
Burial or trenching pass length for pass \(j\)
pass-km


\(q_{\mathrm{bury},j}\)
Operating burial or pre-trenching rate
km/day/pass


\(T_{\mathrm{setup,bury}}\)
Tool deployment and setup time
day


\(T_{\mathrm{reposition,bury}}\)
Positioning between burial passes or sections
day


\(T_{\mathrm{recovery,bury}}\)
Tool recovery time
day



The reviewed ORBIT version 1.3 implementation uses \(q_{\mathrm{bury}}=0.4\) km/h, equivalent to 9.6 km/day of continuous operation, and 0.1 km/h or 2.4 km/day for pre-trenching (National Laboratory of the Rockies, n.d.). Array-cable burial also includes two hours of positioning per section. These are operating defaults rather than achieved campaign rates and must be replaced when route-specific soil and tool evidence are available.
The cable screening case uses 1.5 full-rate-equivalent mobilisation days for the burial vessel, matching the ORBIT cable-vessel proxy. ORBIT does not provide general burial transit, deployment, recovery or demobilisation values; those inputs remain unresolved rather than being silently set to zero.
Burial pass length is not assumed equal to lay pass length. Sections near structures, landfall or designed protection zones may have different burial lengths, but only one physical cable or pipeline is buried in each modeled pass.
Rock, mattresses and crossing structures are excluded from burial-spread time unless the selected burial rate explicitly includes the corresponding installation method and materials. Their material and specialist-package costs normally remain exceptional.
If laying and burial are physically integrated, this separate calculation is not used. The project instead requires one integrated duration and one integrated spread rate.

title: Cable and Pipeline Installation
text:
6. ROV and Survey-Spread Time
The ROV/survey spread can perform independent pre-lay, as-laid, post-burial or inspection campaigns and can support laying, burial or interfaces. Independent survey time is calculated from surveyed pass length and survey rate:
\[
T_{\mathrm{survey,independent,base}}
=
\sum_k
\frac{L_{\mathrm{survey},k}}{q_{\mathrm{survey},k}}
+T_{\mathrm{ROV,interface}}.
\]








Symbol
Definition
Unit




\(T_{\mathrm{survey,independent,base}}\)
Independent survey and interface time before weather uplift
day


\(L_{\mathrm{survey},k}\)
Route or pass length surveyed in activity \(k\)
km


\(q_{\mathrm{survey},k}\)
Operating survey rate for activity \(k\)
km/day


\(T_{\mathrm{ROV,interface}}\)
Independent ROV time at pull-ins, joints, crossings or other interfaces
day



ORBIT’s cable module supplies no independent survey-pass count or survey production rate. These remain site-specific or contractor inputs. For cable screening only, this page uses ORBIT’s generic support vessel as the ROV/survey spread proxy: 10 km/h transit speed, seven full-rate mobilisation days and 113,824 EUR/day (National Laboratory of the Rockies, n.d.). This supplies a provisional cost rate, not the missing survey productivity or proof of a complete commercial survey spread.
ROV support that accompanies another spread is based on that spread’s actual weather-adjusted offshore time:
\[
T_{\mathrm{ROV,support}}
=
\alpha_{\mathrm{lay}}T_{\mathrm{lay,offshore}}
+\alpha_{\mathrm{bury}}T_{\mathrm{bury,offshore}},
\]
where \(\alpha_{\mathrm{lay}}\) and \(\alpha_{\mathrm{bury}}\) are the fractions of lay- and burial-spread offshore time requiring a separately charged ROV/survey spread. They lie between 0 and 1 and must be defined from the installation method.
The reference lay and burial campaigns do not overlap. If support windows do overlap, \(T_{\mathrm{ROV,support}}\) is the duration of their union rather than the arithmetic sum of overlapping days.
Total ROV/survey-spread time is:
\[
T_{\mathrm{ROV}}
=
T_{\mathrm{mob,ROV}}
+T_{\mathrm{demob,ROV}}
+T_{\mathrm{survey,independent}}
+T_{\mathrm{ROV,support}}.
\]
Here \(T_{\mathrm{mob,ROV}}=7\) chargeable days in the cable screening case and \(T_{\mathrm{demob,ROV}}\) remains unresolved. \(T_{\mathrm{survey,independent}}\) is weather-adjusted independent survey time; \(T_{\mathrm{ROV,support}}\) is concurrent support time; and \(T_{\mathrm{ROV}}\) is total chargeable ROV/survey spread-days.
Concurrent support is a separate spread cost, not additional project elapsed time. If ROV and survey equipment are onboard and included in the lay or burial day rate, the corresponding \(\alpha\) is zero and those days are not charged again.

title: Cable and Pipeline Installation
text:
7. Weather and Total Installation CAPEX
Weather is represented by a transparent time uplift rather than an ORBIT discrete-event weather simulation. Port loading and other defined non-weather tasks are not uplifted.
The ORBIT duration used here must therefore exclude simulated weather delay. If a weather-inclusive ORBIT result is used instead, the corresponding uplift \(w\) is set to zero.
For laying:
\[
T_{\mathrm{lay}}
=
T_{\mathrm{lay,nonweather}}
+(1+w_{\mathrm{lay}})
T_{\mathrm{lay,offshore,base}}.
\]
The weather-adjusted lay offshore time used by ROV support is:
\[
T_{\mathrm{lay,offshore}}
=
(1+w_{\mathrm{lay}})
T_{\mathrm{lay,offshore,base}}.
\]
For burial, the model separates any fixed non-weather time from offshore-exposed work:
\[
T_{\mathrm{bury}}
=
T_{\mathrm{bury,nonweather}}
+(1+w_{\mathrm{bury}})
T_{\mathrm{bury,offshore,base}}.
\]
The weather-adjusted burial offshore time used by ROV support is:
\[
T_{\mathrm{bury,offshore}}
=
(1+w_{\mathrm{bury}})
T_{\mathrm{bury,offshore,base}}.
\]
For independent survey:
\[
T_{\mathrm{survey,independent}}
=
(1+w_{\mathrm{ROV}})
T_{\mathrm{survey,independent,base}}.
\]

Unit

Different spreads should use different weather uplifts where evidence permits because their operational limits differ. A common uplift can be used as a transparent screening assumption when better inputs are unavailable.
Once the three chargeable spread times are known, installation CAPEX is:

title: Methodology
text:
This section defines the modelling logic used across all component pages. The model is a deterministic techno-economic optimisation framework for offshore wind systems with alternative energy carriers.
The modelling object is the complete turbine-to-onshore-delivery value chain. The purpose is not to compare isolated component prices, but to represent how component cost, energy conversion, availability, and installation assumptions interact when the energy carrier changes from electricity to hydrogen.

title: Methodology
text:
Methodological Role
The methodology pages define conventions that are shared across components:

the system boundary used for cost and yield accounting
the LCOE objective function
the modelling workflow from fixed inputs to derived parameters and outputs
the optimisation variables treated as model outcomes
the annualisation, energy-basis, and availability conventions used in component calculations

Component-specific assumptions are not collected here. They are documented on the relevant component pages.

title: Methodology
text:
Core Principle
Infrastructure is modelled as part of the offshore energy system, not as an external connection. This matters because export infrastructure is sized for peak capacity but paid back through delivered annual energy. The cost of capacity therefore changes the economically optimal layout and carrier choice.

title: Hydrogen Production
text:
Hydrogen production covers the entire electrolyser. A PEM electrolyser is always assumed in this work.
The electrolyser is split up in the following components:

Stack
Power Electronics
Balance of Plant (BOP)

Note that in most contexts, the balance of plant includes the power electronics, but here they are explicitly treated separately.
The compressor is also not included in this section, but is under Hydrogen Infrastructure: Compressor
The hydrogen production model is dynamic: stack efficiency and auxiliary power consumption depend on operating point, which depends on the wind state and the installed stack capacity.
Finally, note that the exact electrolyser composition depends on the system architecture, with the main difference between central and decentral hydrogen production being the power electronics.

title: DC Integration
text:
The decentralised-hydrogen architecture directly couples a wind-turbine generator to a PEM electrolyser through a shared DC system. The model uses this configuration to remove conversion equipment that is only required for AC export or for supplying a conventional AC-fed electrolyser. The feasibility basis is the Hygro technical assessment of direct DC PEM-wind coupling (Verbist and Damen 2026).
The modelled electrical chain is:
wind-turbine generator -> active rectifier/up-chopper -> DC link -> PEM stack or stack array
The architecture has no AC export connection, turbine grid-side inverter, electrolyser rectifier, or separate electrolyser-side DC/DC converter. The generator-side active rectifier/up-chopper remains part of the turbine and controls generator current, electromagnetic torque, and the power extracted from the rotor.






NoteModel assumption



A dedicated electrolyser-side DC/DC converter is not treated as a fundamental requirement. Its functions are instead allocated to generator power control, generator-stack electrical matching, supervisory operating limits, and coordinated protection. This is an integrated turbine-electrolyser design assumption, not an off-the-shelf equipment configuration.

title: DC Integration
text:
Operating Principle
The generator-side converter controls the electrical power supplied to the PEM system. The PEM polarisation characteristic then establishes the corresponding DC voltage and current. For a single stack, or the equivalent polarisation curve of the active stack array, the operating point satisfies:
\[
P_{\mathrm{gen}}
=
V_{\mathrm{stack}}\!\left(I_{\mathrm{stack}}\right)
I_{\mathrm{stack}}.
\]
where:

\(P_{\mathrm{gen}}\) is the generator electrical power supplied to the DC system, in W;
\(I_{\mathrm{stack}}\) is the total current through the active stack configuration, in A; and
\(V_{\mathrm{stack}}(I_{\mathrm{stack}})\) is the voltage given by its polarisation curve at the applicable temperature, pressure, hydration state, tolerance, and age, in V.

As generator power rises or falls, the operating point moves along the applicable polarisation curve. The DC-link voltage is therefore an operating result rather than the primary controlled variable. Voltage is still measured for operating-envelope supervision, converter limits, and protection, but normal hydrogen production does not require a fixed DC-voltage reference.
This distinction replaces the previous page assumption that an active-front-end voltage loop must hold the DC link at a prescribed value. Even where an active rectifier is used, its normal control objective in this architecture is generator current, torque, and power.

title: DC Integration
text:
Model Calculation
At each operating point, the turbine power command is bounded by the available wind power, generator capability, and the power that the PEM system can safely accept:
\[
P_{\mathrm{cmd}}
=
\min\!\left(
P_{\mathrm{wind,available}},
P_{\mathrm{gen,max}},
P_{\mathrm{PEM,permitted}}
\right).
\]
All four terms are powers in W. The permitted PEM power is a supervisory limit derived from current density, stack temperature and pressure, gas purity, water supply, cooling capacity, and the active stack configuration.
The electrical operating point is then found by solving:
\[
P_{\mathrm{cmd}}
=
V_{\mathrm{stack}}\!\left(I_{\mathrm{stack}}\right)
I_{\mathrm{stack}}
\]
within the permitted current and voltage range. The resulting \(I_{\mathrm{stack}}\) and \(V_{\mathrm{stack}}\) are passed to the PEM stack model to calculate hydrogen production, efficiency, and degradation.
If a modular stack array is used, branch switching changes the equivalent polarisation curve and provides coarse capacity selection. Generator torque remains the continuous power actuator.

Removing the separate stack converter does not remove its required functions. It reallocates them across the integrated system.

title: DC Integration
text:
Feasibility Conditions

Electrical Matching
The full PEM polarisation envelope must remain within the generator-side voltage and current ratings. The check must cover generator speed, stack temperature and pressure, manufacturing tolerance, and ageing. Matching is achieved through the generator winding design, converter range, series cell count, and any stack-array series/parallel configuration.


Boost-Only Constraint
If the generator-side power stage can only raise voltage, the passive rectified generator voltage must remain below the required stack voltage across the permitted speed range. A design that violates this condition would require a buck-capable conversion stage or a different generator-stack match.


Coordinated Control
The PEM controller must provide a continuously updated permitted-power limit. The turbine controller then applies the lowest of available wind power, generator capability, and this PEM limit. Communication failure must lead to a defined safe state rather than continued operation on a stale limit.


Modular Stack Option
A modular array may improve low-load operation, availability, and maintainability. Branch switching can select the active capacity in discrete steps, while generator torque control adjusts power continuously. Modularity is beneficial but is not a prerequisite for the underlying direct-coupling principle.


Start, Stop, and Faults
Turbine current reduction, pitch control, braking, and electrical isolation must be coordinated with PEM start permissives, stack isolation, purge, and safe shutdown. The control design must define timing and authority for start-up, normal stopping, load rejection, communication loss, and emergency shutdown.


Harmonics and Drivetrain Effects
Diode rectification can introduce generator-current harmonics and electromagnetic torque ripple. Generator electromagnetic design, converter thermal loading, and drivetrain loads therefore require validation for the selected topology (Andresen et al. 2025).






WarningUnresolved design input



The repository does not yet provide the project-specific generator winding voltage, speed envelope, rectifier/up-chopper limits, or PEM polarisation envelopes over temperature, pressure, tolerance, and ageing. Until those inputs are available, the model can define the operating-point calculation and equipment boundary but cannot report a verified matched operating envelope.

title: DC Integration
text:
Evidence Base

Direct Proof of Principle
Clarke et al. directly coupled a 2.4 kW photovoltaic array to a PEM electrolyser without an intervening MPPT unit or DC/DC converter. Series-parallel configurations were selected to match the source and electrolyser voltage-current characteristics, and the system accumulated approximately 600 operating hours. This demonstrates that deliberate electrical matching and the PEM polarisation characteristic can establish a stable operating point without an intervening converter (Clarke et al. 2009).
This is proof of the electrical principle, not direct evidence for a multi-megawatt wind turbine.


Wind-Specific Proof of Principle
Chantharasenawong et al. investigated direct coupling of a fixed-pitch, variable-speed aerogenerator to PEM electrolysers without intervening voltage-conversion or maximum-power-point-tracking electronics. The remote-area system is not representative of a modern offshore turbine, but it directly supports matching a wind generator and PEM load (Chantharasenawong et al. 2008).


Industrial Architecture Support
ITM Power and Ørsted proposed placing an electrolyser at an individual Type IV wind turbine and connecting it directly to the turbine DC link. They identify fewer conversion steps, lower losses, a smaller electrolyser footprint, and removal of AC rectification as potential benefits. The publication also states that the system had not been demonstrated in practice, so it supports the intended architecture but does not prove this exact converter arrangement at scale (ITM Power and Ørsted 2020).


Adjacent Electrochemical Precedent
Fraunhofer ICT’s RedoxWind project connects a redox-flow battery directly to the intermediate DC circuit of a 2 MW wind turbine, eliminating an additional conversion step. A battery is not electrically or operationally identical to a PEM electrolyser, but the project validates turbine-level integration of an electrochemical system on a shared DC circuit (Fraunhofer Institute for Chemical Technology ICT, n.d.).


Engineering Qualification
Recent DC wind-turbine research confirms the potential benefit of fewer conversion stages but generally retains high-power DC/DC conversion for voltage adaptation, isolation, and fault handling. This shows that a DC/DC converter may be useful; it does not show that one is inherently required to determine the PEM operating point. The same work identifies current harmonics and torque ripple as validation topics for diode-rectifier concepts (Andresen et al. 2025).

Pipeline Pressure and Capacity
text: Pipeline diameter, inlet pressure, and the number of parallel pipelines are not independent choices. They are three different ways of buying the same thing — hydrogen transport capacity — and each buys it through a different cost centre: pipe material, compressor equipment and energy, or installation. This page sets out how those three costs interact and why the resulting optimum is not smooth.

title: Pipeline Pressure and Capacity
text: Pipeline diameter, inlet pressure, and the number of parallel pipelines are not independent choices. title: Pipeline Pressure and Capacity
text:
Two Ways to Add Capacity
For a fixed pipeline, transport capacity increases with both diameter and pressure drop, but not at the same rate. Diameter enters the capacity relation through the cross-sectional area and the flow velocity together, so capacity scales approximately as \(D^{2.5}\). Pressure enters only through the pressure drop under a square root, so its effect is far weaker and subject to diminishing returns (full derivation in Hydrogen Pipelines).
This asymmetry means diameter and pressure are not equally good levers for the same job, and it is why the two behave so differently in the cost model, not just in the capacity model:

Increasing diameter is the more capacity-effective lever, but it is a step change in material commitment. A larger composite pipeline costs more per metre, and above roughly 8 inch the pipe is assumed to lose the reel-lay flexibility that keeps composite installation cheap in the first place (Hydrogen Pipelines). Past that point, diameter is no longer a lever that can be pulled without also changing the installation method and the cost basis that goes with it.
Increasing pressure adds capacity without any new material or route, but it is equipment- and energy-expensive at the compressor: every bar of additional pressure raises compressor CAPEX and adds a recurring electricity cost for the life of the asset (Hydrogen Compressor).

The same capacity requirement can therefore be met by a fatter pipe running at modest pressure, or a narrower pipe pushed harder by a larger compressor. Which is cheaper is not a property of the pipeline alone; it depends on how the pipe’s material-cost curve compares with the compressor’s cost-and-energy curve over the feasible pressure range.

title: Pipeline Pressure and Capacity
text:
Where Installation Cost Enters
Material and compression are not the whole story, because pipeline capacity is delivered in discrete units. A given diameter-pressure combination yields a fixed maximum flow; if peak hydrogen production exceeds it, the model does not fractionally upsize the pipe — it adds another parallel pipeline. That step adds physical pipe length, interfaces, vessel loads and installation passes.
Installation cost still does not scale as a simple EUR/m coefficient. Parallel lines may share engineering, mobilisation and one broader contractor programme, but each additional line increases the physical installation inventory. The current evidence supports one TCP pipeline per actual lay pass; simultaneous installation of several pipelines must not be assumed without supplier and contractor proof (Cable and Pipeline Installation).
The installation subclass is also tied to the diameter decision. It applies only while the selected pipe remains hydrogen-qualified and compatible with its reel, bend, tension, stability and pull-through limits. Crossing one of those limits can change the vessel, connection concept or pipe technology. Pushing diameter up to avoid another parallel line can therefore trade the discrete cost of an additional pass for a different installation subclass.

title: Pipeline Pressure and Capacity
section: The Resulting Trade-off Is Not Smooth
text:
The Resulting Trade-off Is Not Smooth
Because pipeline count is a ceiling function of required capacity, a small change in peak flow, diameter, or pressure can push a design across the threshold where an extra parallel pipeline becomes necessary — or unnecessary. Near that threshold, the marginal cost of “one more unit of capacity” jumps discontinuously: it can mean a small increase in compressor duty on the existing pipelines, or an entire additional pipeline’s material, interfaces, loads and installation passes.
This is why pressure, diameter, and pipeline count cannot be optimised one at a time. Raising pressure to avoid an extra pipeline only pays off if the resulting compressor cost and energy penalty are smaller than that pipeline’s material and subclass-specific installation cost. Conversely, adding a pipeline only pays off if its complete incremental cost is lower than the compressor cost of reaching the same capacity through pressure alone. The three variables have to be searched jointly over a cost landscape with discrete steps rather than solved as a single continuous minimum.

text:

title: Hydrogen Infield Infrastructure
text:
Proposed Ladder Layout
The proposed network is a ladder. Two longitudinal header pipelines run along opposite sides of the turbine field. Cross-farm pipelines form the rungs. Turbines connect directly to the rung that passes through their row.






Figure 1: Proposed hydrogen infield ladder. The number of rungs and turbines shown is schematic.



The layout is used for four reasons:

A 6 inch composite pipeline at 150 bar is assumed to carry about 500 MW of hydrogen on an HHV-equivalent basis. One rung can therefore collect a complete turbine row without the 60–70 MW string limit of a 66 kV AC cable (Project Team 2026).
Each turbine can send hydrogen to either header. Isolation of one local rung or header segment does not automatically isolate every turbine behind that segment.
The regular grid follows the turbine rows and avoids a separate radial route from every turbine to a central platform.
Flexible composite pipe can be supplied in long reeled lengths. This suits repeated infield runs and reduces the number of offshore field joints relative to rigid steel pipe (Project Team 2026).

The topology provides two infield paths, not two independent export systems. Both paths ultimately reach the same export-pipeline interface. Valves, isolation philosophy and the capacity of the remaining path determine whether the redundancy can be used after a fault.

text:
Pipeline-Length Model
The screening model assumes:

a square wind-farm area;
evenly spaced turbines arranged in approximately square rows;
two headers, each equal to one farm side;
each rung spans one farm side; and
the number of rungs is approximated by the square root of turbine count.

\[
s=\sqrt{A_\mathrm{farm}}.
\]

\[

\]

\[
L_\mathrm{rungs}
=

L_\mathrm{headers}
=

\qquad

\[

L_\mathrm{infield}
&=

title: Hydrogen Infield Infrastructure
Hydrogen Infield Infrastructure
text:
Capacity and Redundancy Checks
The length equation defines geometry only. It does not prove that every segment can carry the required flow.
The 500 MW-equivalent assumption supports the claim that one 6 inch rung can serve a turbine row. Header flow is higher because successive rungs add hydrogen. Header diameter, pressure drop and fault-state capacity must therefore be checked segment by segment. The current model does not yet perform this check and should not assume that every header segment can remain 6 inch.
The same limitation applies to redundancy. An alternative route is useful only if isolation valves can separate the failed section and the remaining pipeline path has enough capacity. The present assumption of 100% infield-pipeline availability is a modelling convention, not a reliability result.

title: Hydrogen Compressor
text:
The hydrogen compressor raises the pressure of produced hydrogen from the PEM electrolyser outlet pressure to the pressure required by the hydrogen pipeline system.
The compressor is modelled explicitly because the pipeline injection pressure is a decision variable in this research. The model must therefore capture how compressor energy consumption and compressor cost change when the selected outlet pressure changes. This is necessary for the pressure-diameter optimisation of the hydrogen pipeline system.
Compression is included only in the hydrogen architectures. In the centralised architecture, compression takes place on the offshore electrolysis platform before injection into the export pipeline. In the decentralised architecture, compression takes place at turbine level before injection into the infield hydrogen pipeline.
The compressor model includes compressor electricity consumption, motor losses, CAPEX, OPEX and availability. It excludes electrolyser stack costs, electrolyser BOP, hydrogen drying, pipeline CAPEX, pipeline pressure drop and onshore recompression.






NoteWhy Outlet Pressure Is Modelled Explicitly



The compressor outlet pressure is the pipeline injection pressure, one of the optimisation variables in this research. Raising it trades cheaper, higher-capacity pipeline transport against a larger compressor energy and CAPEX penalty; see Pipeline Pressure and Capacity for how that trade-off plays out against pipeline diameter, pipeline count, and installation cost.
A fixed compressor energy value would hide that trade-off from the optimisation. This page therefore develops explicit compressor energy and cost models as a function of inlet pressure, outlet pressure, and hydrogen mass flow, so that the optimisation has something to weigh the pipeline side against. See Compression Energy and Cost Model below.

Compressing from 1 bar to 150 bar has a pressure ratio of 150. This is why the relatively high outlet pressure of PEM electrolysers is important for offshore hydrogen systems.

title: Hydrogen Compressor
text:
Compression Energy
The number of compression stages is determined from the maximum allowable pressure ratio per stage:
\[
N =
\left\lceil
\frac{\ln(p_\mathrm{out}/p_\mathrm{in})}
{\ln(r_\mathrm{max})}
\right\rceil
\]
where \(r_\mathrm{max}=3.3\).
The actual pressure ratio per stage is:
\[
r_s =
\left(
\frac{p_\mathrm{out}}{p_\mathrm{in}}
\right)^{1/N}
\]
For the reference case of compression from 30 bar to 150 bar:
\[
\frac{p_\mathrm{out}}{p_\mathrm{in}}
=
\frac{150}{30}
=
5
\]
This gives:
\[
N =
\left\lceil
\frac{\ln(5)}{\ln(3.3)}
\right\rceil
=
2
\]
and:
\[
r_s = 5^{1/2} = 2.24
\]
The compressor shaft work per kg of hydrogen is calculated as:
\[
w_\mathrm{shaft} =
\frac{
N \gamma Z_\mathrm{avg} R T
}{
(\gamma - 1) M_\mathrm{H_2} \eta_\mathrm{comp}
}
\left[
r_s^{(\gamma - 1)/\gamma} - 1
\right]
\]
where \(Z_\mathrm{avg}\) is the average hydrogen compressibility factor between inlet and outlet pressure, evaluated from real-gas hydrogen properties via CoolProp at the arithmetic mean of \(p_\mathrm{in}\) and \(p_\mathrm{out}\), the same way the pipeline capacity model evaluates gas properties at an average pipeline pressure. Hydrogen deviates only mildly from ideal-gas behaviour over this pressure range (\(Z_\mathrm{avg}\) stays within a few percent of 1), but the deviation is calculated rather than assumed.
The electrical energy consumption of the compressor is:
\[
e_\mathrm{comp} =
\frac{
w_\mathrm{shaft}
}{
\eta_\mathrm{motor} \cdot 3.6 \cdot 10^6
}
\]
where \(e_\mathrm{comp}\) is expressed in kWh/kg H₂.
The compressor power demand is then calculated from the hydrogen mass flow rate:
\[
P_\mathrm{comp}
=
e_\mathrm{comp}
\cdot
\dot{m}_\mathrm{H_2}
\]
where \(P_\mathrm{comp}\) is in kW when \(e_\mathrm{comp}\) is in kWh/kg H₂ and \(\dot{m}_\mathrm{H_2}\) is in kg/h.
For annual or time-step calculations, total compressor electricity use is:
\[
E_\mathrm{comp}
=
e_\mathrm{comp}
\cdot
m_\mathrm{H_2}
\]
This energy use is treated as a parasitic load in the hydrogen system.

Sensitivity to Outlet Pressure
Compressor energy consumption increases with outlet pressure because the relevant quantity is the pressure ratio:
\[
\frac{p_\mathrm{out}}{p_\mathrm{in}}
\]
The same outlet pressure can therefore have very different compression penalties depending on electrolyser outlet pressure. Compression to 150 bar is a relatively modest duty when hydrogen leaves the PEM electrolyser at 30 bar, but a much larger duty if hydrogen is produced near atmospheric pressure.
Figure 1 shows \(e_\mathrm{comp}\) across the 80-150 bar outlet-pressure range used elsewhere in the model, for electrolyser outlet pressures of 1, 10, 20 and 30 bar.






Figure 1: Compressor electricity consumption as a function of outlet pressure for different inlet pressures.



The curves confirm why PEM outlet pressure matters: at a given pipeline injection pressure, compressing from 1 bar takes roughly three to four and a half times the electricity of compressing from 30 bar, because it is the pressure ratio that drives compression work, not the absolute pressure difference. Each curve also shows small kinks rather than a smooth rise. These come from the discrete number of compression stages, \(N\): as outlet pressure increases, \(N\) occasionally steps up to keep the per-stage pressure ratio within its 3.3 limit, and each step changes the slope of the curve.

title: Hydrogen Compressor
Hydrogen Compressor
text:
Pressure Optimisation
Pipeline injection pressure is optimised together with pipeline diameter and the number of parallel pipelines, for the reasons set out in Pipeline Pressure and Capacity: pressure, diameter, material cost, and installation cost all move together, so none of them can be picked in isolation.
The optimisation problem is therefore not:
\[
\min e_\mathrm{comp}
\]
and it is also not:
\[
\min C_\mathrm{pipeline}
\]
Instead, the model minimises the combined system cost:
\[
\min_{p_\mathrm{out}, D, n_\mathrm{pipe}}
LCOE
\]
where \(p_\mathrm{out}\) is compressor outlet pressure and pipeline injection pressure, \(D\) is pipeline diameter and \(n_\mathrm{pipe}\) is the number of parallel pipelines.
The optimum can therefore occur at an intermediate pressure. A higher pressure may be justified if it avoids an extra pipeline. A lower pressure may be preferable if the pipeline is already oversized and additional compression provides little transport benefit.

title: Onshore Grid Connection
text:
Physical Layout
At landfall, the submarine cable is brought ashore through an open trench or, more commonly at sensitive coastlines, ducts installed by horizontal directional drilling. Submarine and land cable designs are connected in accessible transition-joint bays. The separate pole, metallic-return and communication cables then continue underground to the converter site.
The onshore converter changes DC power back to three-phase AC. Converter transformers provide voltage transformation and electrical separation, while reactors, filters and controls manage current, harmonics, voltage and reactive power. High-voltage switchgear connects the station to the transmission grid and isolates equipment for faults and maintenance.
TenneT describes the Dutch 2 GW interface as 525 kV DC conversion to 380 kV AC. Its standard onshore arrangement has six single-phase converter transformers plus one spare (TenneT 2024). For the Doordewind connection, TenneT reports an onshore converter-station footprint of roughly 5.5 ha before the underground connection to the 380 kV substation (TenneT, n.d.). The land requirement reflects electrical clearances, converter halls, cooling, transformers, roads, drainage, security and construction space; it is not just the building footprint.

title: Onshore Grid Connection
text:
Electrical Rating
AC equipment must carry more than active MW alone:

active power \(P\), measured in MW, transfers net energy and is what the wind farm is primarily selling;
reactive power \(Q\), measured in MVAr, oscillates between electric and magnetic fields and is used to control AC voltage; and
apparent power \(S\), measured in MVA, combines both and determines much of the current and thermal loading of transformers, converters and switchgear.

Power factor is \(P/S\). A value below one means some equipment current is being used for reactive rather than active power.
At unity power factor, the AC line current associated with 2 GW at 380 kV is:
\[
I_\mathrm{AC}
=
\frac{P}{\sqrt{3}V_\mathrm{LL}\cos\phi}
=
\frac{2{,}000\times10^6}
{\sqrt{3}(380\times10^3)}
=3.04\ \mathrm{kA}.
\]
The station is not designed as one 3 kA conductor. Power is divided among converter transformer windings, bus sections and grid circuits so equipment ratings, fault levels and maintenance criteria can be satisfied.
Reactive-power operation increases apparent power:
\[
S=\frac{P}{\cos\phi},
\qquad
Q=\sqrt{S^2-P^2}.
\]
If 2 GW were delivered at a power factor of 0.95, the terminal duty would be about 2.105 GVA and 657 MVAr. This is an illustration, not a selected grid-code operating point. Actual reactive capability is specified as a voltage-dependent envelope and can require converter-current headroom, reactors or additional compensation.
The grid-connection study must check at least:

rated and temporary voltage ranges;
active-power ramping and frequency response;
reactive-power and voltage-control capability;
fault ride-through and post-fault active-power recovery;
harmonic emission and resonance;
short-circuit level and protection coordination;
maximum permissible loss of infeed.

Several of these terms describe different questions. Fault level is the current the surrounding grid can supply into a short circuit; it affects switchgear duty and converter-control behaviour, not how often faults occur. Fault ride-through asks whether the link remains connected during a temporary voltage depression. Harmonics are unwanted waveform components that can cause heating, resonance or interference. A strong grid node is one whose voltage and stability remain acceptable when 2 GW changes or trips–not merely one with high annual energy demand.
Commission Regulation (EU) 2016/1447 sets the European HVDC framework for these active-power, reactive-power, voltage, fault-ride-through, control, protection and monitoring capabilities (European Commission 2016). Project-specific requirements are then agreed with the relevant transmission-system operator.
The current Dutch system code adds useful numerical context at the point of connection (Government of the Netherlands 2026):

text:
Capacity and Connection Architecture
The HVDC link is sized in discrete 2 GW blocks in the reference model:
\[
n_\mathrm{link}
=
\left\lceil
\frac{P_\mathrm{export}}{2{,}000\ \mathrm{MW}}
\right\rceil.

This does not prove that the receiving grid can accept \(2n_\mathrm{link}\) GW at the selected PCC. A grid study determines whether existing 380 kV circuits have sufficient thermal, voltage and stability margin and whether a new substation, busbar extension, underground cable or overhead-line reinforcement is required.
The connection point can therefore drive project economics independently of offshore distance. A shorter sea route to a weak grid node may require more onshore reinforcement than a longer route to a strong node. The model should treat:

dedicated connection assets from landfall to the agreed grid point; and
wider network reinforcement triggered beyond that point

as separate cost categories. Their payer and regulatory treatment may also differ.

text:
Conversion and Transformer Losses
The current model fills the previously blank onshore efficiency with a provisional aggregate 98.5%. This covers the onshore converter, converter transformers and station auxiliaries once. Hitachi Energy reports conversion losses below 1% per station for the 900 MW DolWin2 VSC system (Hitachi Energy, n.d.), supporting the order of magnitude but not establishing a 2 GW guarantee.
Large-transformer efficiency regulation provides another useful check. For liquid-immersed large transformers, the European Tier 2 minimum peak-efficiency index is 99.770% at 100 MVA, rises with rating and reaches 99.797% at 200 MVA and above (European Commission 2014). title: About
text:
This site documents the assumptions behind a component-level techno-economic model for offshore wind infrastructure.
The model compares electricity-based export, centralised offshore hydrogen production, and decentralised turbine-integrated hydrogen production. The source material is a set of working Word documents in background/. Some assumptions rely on internal supplier or manufacturer data; those are documented at the level needed for model reproducibility without exposing confidential raw datasets.

Infield, inter-array or array cables form the medium-voltage collection network inside the wind farm. Each radial string carries the output of several turbines to an offshore AC bus. The cables are used by both the electricity-export and centralised-hydrogen architectures; decentralised hydrogen replaces the main array network with hydrogen pipelines.

This page covers cable supply only. Cable-lay vessels, route preparation, burial, pull-ins and other installation activities are costed separately on Cable and Pipeline Installation.






NotePhysical picture: a radial electrical tree



An array string is comparable to a daisy chain. The first cable segment carries one turbine’s output; each following segment carries that turbine plus every turbine farther from the substation. The final segment into the offshore bus therefore carries the greatest current and usually needs the largest conductor.
The reference design is radial: there is one normal path from each turbine to the substation. This is simple and economical, but a fault near the root of a string can disconnect all turbines downstream of it. A ring or meshed network could provide another path, at the cost of more cable and switchgear.

title: Infield AC Cables
section: Why 66 kV Is the Reference Voltage
text:
Why 66 kV Is the Reference Voltage
Moving from 33 kV to 66 kV approximately doubles the transferable power at the same current. That allows more turbine capacity per string, fewer strings and fewer offshore-platform entries. Carbon Trust estimated that the transition could reduce offshore-wind LCOE by about 1.5%, and DNV GL’s TenneT study found a material reduction in cable length for the Dutch Borssele concept (Carbon Trust 2014; DNV GL 2015).
The technology is now demonstrated at commercial scale. Borssele 1 and 2 used three-phase 66 kV copper array cables in two cross-sections over roughly 170–190 km (Nexans 2018). Fixed 66 kV-class submarine cables fall within the scope of IEC 63026, while project design must also address offshore-specific interfaces, installation and mechanical loading (International Electrotechnical Commission 2019; DNV, n.d.).
66 kV should nevertheless be treated as the current reference, not a permanent optimum. Carbon Trust’s later high-voltage-array work considers 132 kV as turbine and plant ratings grow; it reported modelled savings of GBP 32–50 million for a 1,200 MW future plant relative to an equivalent 66 kV system (Carbon Trust 2022).

title: Infield AC Cables
text:
String Capacity Model
For target farm capacity \(P_\mathrm{target}\) and turbine rating \(P_\mathrm{turb}\), the installed turbine count and capacity are:
\[
N_\mathrm{turb}
=
\left\lceil
\frac{P_\mathrm{target}}{P_\mathrm{turb}}
\right\rceil,
\qquad
P_\mathrm{farm}
=
N_\mathrm{turb}P_\mathrm{turb}.
\]
For a selected usable string rating, the number of full turbines that fit on one radial string is:
\[
n_\mathrm{turb/string}
=
\left\lfloor
\frac{P_\mathrm{string}}{P_\mathrm{turb}}
\right\rfloor,
\]
and the minimum number of strings is:
\[
n_\mathrm{string}
=
\left\lceil
\frac{N_\mathrm{turb}}{n_\mathrm{turb/string}}
\right\rceil.
\]
The floor operator in the first equation prevents a fraction of a turbine being assigned to a string. The ceiling operator in the second ensures that a partly filled final string still receives a complete cable, switchgear bay and platform termination. These discrete jumps are why a small change in turbine or string rating can create a noticeable CAPEX step.
This is the same basic capacity logic used by NREL’s ORBIT model (Nunemaker et al. 2020). Final cable selection must also check voltage drop, short-circuit duty, charging current, burial depth, seabed thermal resistivity, conductor temperature, armour losses and post-installation protection.






NoteWorked example: 15 MW turbines



Four 15 MW turbines place 60 MW on a string. Five place 75 MW on it and exceed the 64–66 MW screening range. A nominal 2 GW target therefore requires 134 turbines, giving 2.01 GW installed and:
\[
n_\mathrm{string}=\left\lceil\frac{134}{4}\right\rceil=34.
\]


Figure 1 shows the resulting discrete string count. A small increase in plant capacity can require a complete additional feeder, switchgear bay, J-tube, pull-in and cable route.






Figure 1: Required 66 kV radial strings for 15 MW turbines and a 64–66 MW usable string rating.









WarningThe worked array does not fit the reference platform unchanged



TenneT’s 2 GW reference arrangement shows 24 dedicated wind-farm bays plus four universal bays (TenneT 2024). The 34-string worked case therefore needs at least six more terminations than the maximum 28 shown, even if every universal bay is assigned to a feeder. A consistent design must do one or more of the following:

adopt a cable and platform interface rated for at least 75 MW per string, so five 15 MW turbines fit and only 27 strings are required;
add offshore feeder aggregation or another switchgear interface;
move to a higher collection voltage; or
use a project-specific platform layout with more bays.

This interface constraint must be solved before the 34-string cable count and standard 2 GW platform are combined in one cost case.

title: Infield AC Cables
text:
Cable-Length Model
Cable length is calculated from the modelled turbine layout and radial-string topology. Capacity determines the number of turbines and strings; rotor diameter and spacing determine their separation; farm area, aspect ratio and substation position constrain the coordinates. This keeps cable length responsive when any of those design inputs change.
For rotor diameter \(D\) in metres and along-string and cross-string spacings \(s_x\) and \(s_y\) in rotor diameters, the physical spacings are:
\[
d_x=\frac{s_xD}{1000},
\qquad
d_y=\frac{s_yD}{1000},
\]
where \(d_x\) and \(d_y\) are in kilometres. The wind-layout model places \(N_\mathrm{turb}\) turbines inside the farm boundary using these spacings and returns turbine coordinates \((x_j,y_j)\). The gross farm area \(A_\mathrm{farm}\), spacing and turbine count are not independent: the selected coordinates must satisfy both the minimum-spacing rules and the site boundary. The model must flag an infeasible combination rather than silently rescale the spacing.
For an ideal rectangular grid with \(n_x\) turbine positions along the wind direction and \(n_y\) across it, where \(n_xn_y\geq N_\mathrm{turb}\), the occupied grid spans are:
\[
W_\mathrm{grid}=(n_x-1)d_x,
\qquad
H_\mathrm{grid}=(n_y-1)d_y.
\]
These spans, together with boundary margins and exclusions, must fit inside \(A_\mathrm{farm}\). Farm area is therefore a geometric constraint, not an additional cable-length multiplier. A larger boundary changes cable length only when the layout actually spreads the turbine coordinates farther apart.
The string-capacity calculation above partitions the turbines into radial strings with no more than \(n_\mathrm{turb/string}\) turbines. Let \(\mathcal{E}\) be the resulting set of cable connections: one connection from the offshore substation to the first turbine on each string, followed by turbine-to-turbine connections. The horizontal distance of connection \((u,v)\) is:
\[
d_{uv}
=
\sqrt{(x_u-x_v)^2+(y_u-y_v)^2}.
\]
Total pre-route horizontal cable length is therefore:
\[
L_\mathrm{horizontal}
=
\sum_{(u,v)\in\mathcal{E}}d_{uv},
\]
and the screening supply length is:
\[
L_\mathrm{array}
=
(1+r)L_\mathrm{horizontal}
+
L_\mathrm{pull\text{-}in},
\]
where \(r\) is the route allowance and \(L_\mathrm{pull\text{-}in}\) is the separately calculated total cable length between seabed touchdown points and turbine or platform terminations. No default pull-in length is inserted until the water-depth and interface assumptions are defined.
This is the same calculation structure used by ORBIT’s grid-array model: turbine and row spacing define coordinates, cable capacity limits turbines per string, and the model sums the Euclidean distance between successive connection points (Nunemaker et al. 2020).

title: Infield AC Cables
text:
OPEX Allowance
Public evidence describes large but infrequent cable failures more clearly than it reports expected annual cable-only expenditure. ORE Catapult’s SPARTA portfolio found cable outages in 7.46% of wind-farm months and in 61% of reporting wind farms, with outage days split approximately equally between array and export cables (ORE Catapult 2022). Its ELECTRODE programme reports an average repair duration of about two months and consequences often above GBP 10 million, but that amount combines repair expenditure and lost generation (ORE Catapult 2023).
These data do not provide an array-only annual failure frequency or a clean split between physical repair cost and lost revenue. An event-based OPEX model is therefore not used. The current relationship is retained as a top-down risk allowance:
\[
C_\mathrm{OPEX}
=
f_\mathrm{OPEX}C_\mathrm{supply},
\]
with \(f_\mathrm{OPEX}=2\%\)/year and a 1–3% sensitivity. At the base cable price, each 100 km of supplied cable has EUR 40 million supply CAPEX and therefore a EUR 0.8 million annual allowance. The allowance represents inspection and physical repair provision only. Lost generation remains in the availability calculation and must not also be included in OPEX.

title: Infield AC Cables
text:
Reliability and Availability
The current model applies 99.0% array-network availability as a flat annual yield multiplier. A radial string fault normally disconnects the turbines downstream of the fault rather than the complete wind farm, so the flat multiplier does not represent topology explicitly.
No more detailed failure model is introduced until consistent array-specific failure frequency, repair duration and affected-capacity data are available. When those inputs exist, the radial connections \(\mathcal{E}\) defined by the cable-length model can also define the turbines isolated by each fault. Until then, 99.0% remains a transparent aggregate assumption rather than a calculated reliability result.

title: Hydrogen Pipelines
text:
Composite Flexible Pipelines
Composite flexible pipelines are used as the reference hydrogen pipeline technology in this model. A flexible composite pipe typically combines a hydrogen-compatible liner, load-bearing composite reinforcement, and a protective outer layer. Compared with a rigid steel pipeline, the relevant system-level advantage is not only material substitution. The important offshore feature is that the pipe can be manufactured and transported in long continuous lengths, spooled on a reel, and laid with fewer welded field joints.
This matters for offshore hydrogen infrastructure because the model is concerned with many repeated infield connections and, in the decentralised architecture, a pipeline grid that replaces the AC infield cable network. Flexible composite lines are lighter than steel lines at the diameters considered here, are less exposed to corrosion-related design issues, and can simplify installation logistics. These advantages are especially relevant for infield pipelines and for export pipelines up to the diameter range that remains compatible with reel-lay handling.
The flexibility benefit is not unlimited. Larger diameters and higher pressure classes require more reinforcement and increase minimum bend radius. The source material therefore caps the composite export-pipeline diameter at 8 inch: above this range, the pipeline is assumed to lose the reel-lay flexibility that motivates the technology choice (Project Team 2026).

Confidentiality Handling
The raw supplier quotes and fitted material-cost surface are confidential. They are used only to parameterise the model and are not reproduced in this encyclopedia page. Figures derived from them show pressure and diameter on their true scale, since those are model inputs, not supplier data. The cost axis is left without tick labels so that only the shape of the cost curves, not the underlying price level, is disclosed.


Material Cost vs. Pressure
Figure 2 shows pipeline material cost as a function of inlet pressure, for the same diameters used in Figure 1. Cost increases sharply from one diameter class to the next, which is expected for a larger pipe, but at fixed diameter the increase with pressure is comparatively small. Material cost, in other words, is mainly a diameter decision. It is capacity, not material cost, that responds strongly to pressure, which is why pressure and diameter play such different roles in the trade-off described in Pipeline Pressure and Capacity: raising pressure is cheap on the pipe itself, and its real cost shows up at the compressor instead (Hydrogen Compressor).






Figure 2: Hydrogen export-pipeline material cost as a function of inlet pressure and diameter.





Cost per Unit of Transport Capacity
Figure 3 divides the cost curves in Figure 2 by the capacity curves in Figure 1, giving material cost per unit of transport capacity at each diameter and pressure.
Because capacity scales much more strongly with diameter than material cost does, cost per unit capacity falls as diameter increases. This is the basis for the earlier claim that the economic optimum tends toward the largest feasible composite diameter. The same ratio also falls with pressure, at diminishing rate, for the same reason: on the pipe alone, more pressure buys more capacity for very little extra material cost. This curve reflects material cost only. It does not include the compressor cost and energy penalty that pressure also brings, which is why a pure cost-per-capacity view of the pipeline cannot be used to pick a pressure on its own — see Pipeline Pressure and Capacity for how the compressor side of that trade-off is brought back in.






Figure 3: Hydrogen export-pipeline material cost per unit of transport capacity, as a function of inlet pressure and diameter.

title: Hydrogen Infrastructure
text:
Hydrogen infrastructure covers everything that moves hydrogen from the electrolyser outlet to the onshore interface: compression, and the pipeline network that carries the gas offshore and to shore.
The section is split into:

Hydrogen Infield Infrastructure — ladder topology for the decentralised architecture and the calculation of total infield pipeline length.
Hydrogen Compressor — raises hydrogen from electrolyser outlet pressure to the pipeline injection pressure, with the associated electricity consumption, CAPEX, and OPEX.
Hydrogen Pipelines — composite flexible pipeline technology, diameter and pressure sizing, transport capacity, and material cost, for both the infield network and the export route.
Pipeline Pressure and Capacity — how pipeline diameter, inlet pressure, and installation cost trade off against each other in sizing the pipeline system.

Compressor and pipeline assumptions are coupled rather than independent: higher inlet pressure increases compressor energy consumption and cost but also increases pipeline capacity, which can reduce the number of parallel pipelines required. Pipeline count in turn interacts with installation cost, because a single lay vessel can install multiple pipelines together. Pressure, diameter, and pipeline count are therefore optimised jointly rather than one at a time.
The current hydrogen infrastructure model assumes no additional hydrogen losses in pipelines after compression.

Scaling Method
The BOP is not assumed to scale linearly with installed capacity. Water treatment, cooling, gas-liquid separation, drying, piping and instrumentation can be shared across multiple stacks. A centralised or semi-centralised BOP system is therefore expected to be cheaper than many small independent BOP systems with the same total capacity.
Because the exact scaling exponent is not known, the model uses the six-tenths rule as a first-order process-equipment scaling approximation. The six-tenths rule is a standard preliminary process-equipment cost-scaling method in which cost scales with capacity using an exponent close to 0.6 (Engineering LibreTexts, n.d.; Peters et al., n.d.).

Under this scaling assumption, a more centralised BOP architecture is cheaper than a highly decentralised architecture with the same total electrolyser capacity. The scaling rule should therefore be interpreted as an early-stage approximation rather than a detailed equipment design. BOP Power Consumption
The BOP also consumes electricity during electrolyser operation. This consumption is treated separately from stack electricity consumption.
The BOP power consumption represents parasitic loads from auxiliary systems such as pumps, fans, chillers, recirculation blowers, thermal management and hydrogen drying.
Compression is excluded from this value because compression is represented elsewhere in the model. Electrical conversion losses are also explicitly excluded because power electronics are represented separately.
The NREL report cites a generic BOP electricity consumption of 4.2 kWh/kg H₂ (Table 1), but this value includes electrical losses and is therefore not directly applicable to the non-electrical BOP scope used here (Badgett et al. 2024).

Offshore desalination and water polishing are small compared with the main BOP parasitic loads. title: Power Electronics
text:
Reference Architecture
The reference configuration is a water-cooled, 24-pulse thyristor rectifier supplied through a phase-shifting rectifier transformer. Multi-pulse thyristor conversion remains a common industrial solution at multi-megawatt scale because it combines high efficiency, low semiconductor cost, high current capability, and established reliability. Contemporary commercial systems are offered in 6-, 12-, 18-, and 24-pulse arrangements, with harmonic distortion decreasing as pulse number increases (ABB 2025). Reviews of large-scale electrolyser converters likewise identify thyristor rectifiers as the established high-power option, while active-front-end and chopper-based systems trade higher cost and conversion complexity for improved power quality and controllability (Yodwong et al. 2020; Chen et al. 2022).
The 66 kV input is represented as an aggregated two-stage voltage reduction:
\[
66\ \mathrm{kV\ AC}
\rightarrow
\mathrm{medium\mbox{-}voltage\ AC}
\rightarrow
\mathrm{controlled\ stack\ DC}.
\]
The intermediate voltage and detailed transformer winding arrangement are not modelled. Large-plant studies use comparable high-voltage-to-medium-voltage distribution followed by repeated transformer–rectifier modules, including PEM layouts based on approximately 40 MW power blocks (Noordende and Ripson 2020).
